metaDescription: Six Chromebooks at or under $300 compared on screen, storage, processor and size for school, email, video calls and everyday browsing at home.
introParagraphs: A Chromebook under the lower cap is a simple proposition: a laptop that does web browsing, email, documents, video calls and streaming, and does not ask much of you in return. The catch is that cheap models vary a lot in the places that matter, namely the screen, the storage and the amount of memory behind the browser tabs.

The six machines here cover every common size, from an 11.6 inch student model to a 15.6 inch laptop with a full keyboard. Some have touchscreens, some fold into tablets, and one has a sharper full HD panel. We evaluated each from the specs and buyer feedback in its listing, and we call out where the pages leave a detail unspecified, because a vague listing is a risk at this level.

The practical question is what you can safely give up. Many buyers can live with a basic screen or modest storage, but few are happy with 16 GB of flash or a cramped 11.6 inch panel once the novelty fades. We point out which compromises are comfortable and which are traps. As a rule, resolution and storage are the two that cannot be fixed later, while a slightly slow chip can be worked around by keeping fewer tabs open. Keep that rule in mind as you read the picks, and use the later sections to match a model to the person who will actually use it, whether that is a student, a parent or a grandparent.

products.name: Lenovo Flagship 14 Inch FHD Touchscreen Chromebook
products.description:
Lenovo gives this Chromebook the best screen in the group, a 14 inch full HD touchscreen with 1920 x 1080 resolution. Under the hood is a MediaTek Kompanio 520, an eight-core design with four A73 cores and four A53 cores at 2.0GHz, paired with 4GB of RAM and 64GB of eMMC storage.

The sharper display is what you notice every day, since text is crisper and video looks better than on the typical 1366 x 768 panels at this level. The processor is designed for battery life as much as speed, which suits a laptop used for browsing and documents. The touchscreen is a plus for tapping through Android apps and for anyone who prefers direct input.

Compared with the Acer, it trades screen size for portability, and compared with the HP 14 at N4120 it offers a better display but no stated battery figure. Its main limit is 4GB of RAM, so keep tab counts reasonable. It is a strong all-rounder for students and adults alike.
products.bestFor: Anyone who wants the sharpest screen and a touchscreen.
pros: Full HD touchscreen sharper than rivals
Eight-core MediaTek Kompanio 520 chip
64GB storage gives room for files
Slim 14 inch body suits travel
cons: 4GB RAM limits heavy tab use somewhat
Battery hours are not stated on the listing

products.name: Acer 15.6 Inch FHD Chromebook with Numeric Keypad
products.description:
Acer takes the opposite approach to the compact models: a 15.6 inch full HD display, a full-size keyboard with a dedicated numeric keypad, and a dual-core Intel Celeron processor. It ships with 64GB of storage, WiFi 6 and a carrying sleeve, and runs ChromeOS with built-in Gemini AI features.

The big screen and numpad make it ideal for spreadsheet work, long documents and anyone who needs to see more on screen. Dual-core processors are fine for web apps but slower than quad-core options, so heavy multitasking will stretch it. Size also means weight, and a 15.6 inch laptop is less comfortable to carry than the 11.6 inch models.

Next to the Lenovo Flagship it offers a larger screen but no touch, and next to the HP 14 N4120 it has the bigger display with a weaker processor. It suits a home-base laptop that sits on a desk or kitchen table more than a backpack.
products.bestFor: Home users who want a big screen and a numeric keypad.
pros: Large 15.6 inch full HD display
Full-size keyboard with numeric keypad
WiFi 6 and a carrying sleeve included
64GB storage leaves room for local files
cons: Dual-core Celeron is the slowest chip
Bulkier to carry than 14 inch models
No touchscreen mentioned on the listing

products.name: HP 14 Inch HD Chromebook for Students N4120
products.description:
HP builds this 14 inch student model around a quad-core Intel Celeron N4120, with a 1.1GHz base clock that boosts up to 2.6GHz. It comes with 4GB of RAM, 64GB of eMMC storage, a webcam and an HDMI port, and a rated battery life of 14 hours.

The webcam and long rated battery make it a natural pick for video calls with family or for a student who moves between classes. The processor offers four cores and threads, so it feels more responsive than the dual-core Acer when you open several tabs. The display is a standard HD panel, which is serviceable rather than sharp.

Compared with the Lenovo Flagship, it has a plainer screen but a more conventional Intel chip and a stated battery figure. Against the Dell at 11.6 inches, it offers far more storage and a larger display. It is the safe middle choice for users who want dependable basics.
products.bestFor: Students and seniors who value battery life and video calls.
pros: Quad-core N4120 handles several tabs
Rated for 14 hours of battery life
Webcam and HDMI port built into the body
64GB storage is generous at this level
cons: HD screen is plain compared with FHD
Not a touchscreen or convertible design

products.name: HP Chromebook 14 Intel Celeron N4120
products.description:
This HP Chromebook 14 shares the quad-core N4120 and the 4GB and 64GB combination with its student sibling, but it pitches itself at home, work and school with a thin design and custom-tuned stereo speakers. The micro-edge, anti-glare 14 inch display runs at 1366 x 768.

The anti-glare finish helps in bright rooms and near windows, which makes it more pleasant than a glossy panel for long sessions. The speakers are a small upgrade for streaming and calls. The resolution is the weak spot: text and video are less crisp than on a full HD screen, which you notice most on documents.

Placed next to the HP student model, it is almost the same machine in spec terms, so choose by design and features. Compared with the Lenovo Flagship, it gives up resolution and touch but keeps a familiar Intel platform. It is a practical choice for households that want dependable basics.
products.bestFor: Households that want a thin, anti-glare laptop for daily use.
pros: Anti-glare screen helps in bright rooms
Quad-core N4120 with 64GB storage
Custom-tuned stereo speakers on board
Thin design is easy to carry around
cons: 4GB RAM is tight with many tabs
Almost identical to the HP student model

products.name: Lenovo 300e 11.6 Inch Touchscreen 2-in-1 Chromebook
products.description:
The 300e is a classroom-style convertible with an 11.6 inch IPS touchscreen that supports 10-point multitouch, a quad-core MediaTek 8173C at 2.1GHz, 4GB of LPDDR3 memory and up to 32GB of eMMC storage. The 2-in-1 design flips the screen around for tablet use.

The IPS panel offers wider viewing angles than basic displays, and the flip hinge makes it handy for reading, drawing and shared viewing. The processor is older than the Intel and Kompanio chips in this lineup, and 32GB of storage fills up quickly with downloads. It is best viewed as a light, flexible secondary device.

Compared with the Dell, it offers a touchscreen and double the storage, though both share an 11.6 inch size. Next to the HP 14 models, it trades screen size and speed for flexibility. It is a good fit for kids, couches and anyone who wants a tablet-style Chromebook without a separate tablet.
products.bestFor: Kids and casual users who like a flip-over touchscreen.
pros: Flips into tablet mode for reading
IPS panel offers wide viewing angles
10-point multitouch for drawing and play
Compact 11.6 inch size suits small hands

products.name: Dell Chromebook 11 3100 with Celeron N4020
products.description:
Dell's 3100 is the smallest and most basic machine in this lineup. It pairs an Intel Celeron N4020 with 4GB of RAM and 16GB of flash storage behind an 11.6 inch display at 1366 x 768. It runs ChromeOS, and the compact size is designed for classroom use.

The small body makes it easy to carry and stow in a crowded bag, and the plain feature list means there is little to learn or troubleshoot. The big compromise is storage: 16GB is tight even by Chromebook standards, and updates plus a few Android apps will leave little room for downloads. You will rely on cloud storage for almost everything.

Compared with the HP 14 models, it offers a smaller screen and a third of the storage, which is the price of compactness. It is a reasonable pick for someone who treats it as a browser terminal and keeps files in the cloud, but a poor choice for offline use.
products.bestFor: Cloud-first users who prize a small, light laptop.
pros: Compact 11.6 inch size is easy to carry
Celeron N4020 handles basic browsing
Classroom-oriented model with a plain feature set
ChromeOS keeps boot and updates simple
cons: 16GB storage is very tight for updates

buyingCriteria.explanation: A full HD panel at 1920 x 1080 is noticeably sharper than the 1366 x 768 screens common at this level. The Lenovo Flagship and Acer both offer FHD, while the HP Chromebook 14, Dell and Lenovo 300e use the lower resolution. IPS panels, like the 300e's, improve viewing angles. If you read a lot, put resolution near the top of your list. Also look at the size of the bezel and the finish: anti-glare coatings, like the one on the HP Chromebook 14, cut reflections near windows, while glossy panels look punchier but struggle in bright rooms.

Chrome OS leans on the cloud, but updates, offline files and Android apps still take space. The Dell has 16GB, the 300e up to 32GB and the others 64GB. Anything under 32GB gets crowded fast. Plan on 64GB if you store photos or documents locally. Even cloud-first users benefit from headroom, because a drive that is nearly full slows updates and can fail to install new apps without warning.

A quad-core Intel N4120, as in the two HP models, feels livelier with tabs than the dual-core Celeron in the Acer or the N4020 in the Dell. The Kompanio 520 in the Lenovo Flagship is efficient. All six use 4GB of RAM, so tabs are the limit, not the chip. Closing unused tabs and pausing background Android apps recovers more speed than any processor difference between these models, and a quick restart once a week keeps memory tidy.

Screen sizes range from 11.6 inch (Dell, 300e) to 14 inch (Lenovo Flagship, both HPs) and 15.6 inch (Acer). Smaller screens are lighter but cramp documents. A 14 inch panel is the best balance for most people, while the Acer suits a mostly stationary setup.

A touchscreen helps with Android apps, reading and drawing. The Lenovo Flagship offers touch on a laptop body, and the 300e flips into tablet mode. If you only type and browse, skip touch and spend the budget on a better display.

Battery claims vary with workload. The HP 14 student model lists 14 hours, while others do not state a figure. A webcam matters for video calls, and the HP 14 includes one. Check the listing for the specific hardware before buying, and remember that rated hours come from light-use tests, so a video-heavy day will drain it sooner than the headline number suggests.

howWeEvaluated.title: Display quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared resolution, size and panel type. The Lenovo Flagship and Acer led with 1920 x 1080, the 300e earned credit for IPS, and the Dell and HP 14 Chromebook scored lower at 1366 x 768.

howWeEvaluated.title: Processor and memory
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed the cores and clock speeds listed: quad-core N4120 on both HPs, the eight-core Kompanio 520 on the Lenovo, dual-core Celeron on the Acer and N4020 on the Dell. All sit at 4GB of RAM, so no model scored highly for multitasking.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored 64GB on the Lenovo Flagship, Acer and both HPs, and penalized 32GB on the 300e and 16GB on the Dell, since storage is hard to fix after purchase.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability and design
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered weight cues, size and form factor. The 300e's flip hinge and the Dell's compact body scored for portability, while the Acer's 15.6 inch size scored for desk use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Everyday extras
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted webcams, speakers, ports and battery claims. The HP 14 student model's webcam and 14 hour rating stood out, and the Acer's WiFi 6 and numeric keypad added value. Where a listing left out the battery rating or port list, we did not credit the model, since an unstated feature cannot be relied on when the order arrives.

faq.q: Which Chromebook under this cap is the best overall?
faq.a: The Lenovo Flagship 14 inch is the best all-rounder because of its full HD touchscreen, 64GB of storage and an efficient Kompanio 520 chip. The HP 14 student model is the better choice if battery life and a webcam matter most.

For browsing, documents and streaming, yes, if you keep tab counts reasonable. All six here use 4GB, so tab hoarders will slow down regardless of chip. If you work with many windows, consider spending more for 8GB.
On the Dell it is tight. Chrome OS updates and Android apps use space, leaving little for offline files. Use cloud storage and an SD card if the port exists, or choose a 64GB model.

Only if you will use it. Touch helps with Android apps, reading and drawing, and the Lenovo Flagship and 300e offer it. For typing and browsing, a better non-touch display is a smarter use of the budget.

faq.q: How long will a budget Chromebook receive updates?
faq.a: Chromebooks receive updates for a fixed period from the platform's release, and older models stop sooner. Check Google's automatic update expiration for the exact model before buying, especially for older chips like the 300e's.

faq.q: Can I use these for Microsoft Office?
faq.a: Yes, through web versions and Android apps, though features are more limited than desktop software. Documents, sheets and slides open fine for typical use, but advanced macros will not run.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake buyers make here?
faq.a: Choosing on size or color and ignoring storage and resolution. A cheap model with 16GB or a dim 1366 x 768 screen becomes frustrating within months. Compare the three numbers: resolution, storage and RAM. It also pays to check the auto update expiration date for the exact model, since a laptop that stops getting updates early becomes a security risk long before it stops working.
